subject: Julius Caesar
overview: Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman, and author who conquered Gaul and defeated his rival Pompey in a civil war to become dictator of Rome. After receiving the title dictator perpetuo, he was assassinated by senators who hoped to restore the Roman Republic. Instead, his murder sparked new civil wars that led to the rise of his adopted heir Augustus and the Roman Empire.

key_moments.title: The First Triumvirate and Gaul
key_moments.text: Caesar forged an informal political alliance—the **First Triumvirate**—with **Pompey** and **Crassus** to outmaneuver conservative rivals in the Senate. He then spent years campaigning in the **Gallic Wars**, expanding Roman territory across Gaul, bridging the Rhine, and launching invasions of Britain. Those victories brought him immense wealth and a fiercely loyal veteran army, alarming senators and fracturing his alliance with Pompey.

key_moments.title: Crossing the Rubicon
key_moments.text: When the Senate ordered him to give up his military command and return to Rome, Caesar defied the order and led his army across the **Rubicon**, the river marking the boundary of his province. According to the Roman biographer Suetonius, he paused at the stream to warn his companions that once they crossed that little bridge, the entire issue belonged to the sword, before declaring that **the die was cast** and plunging Rome into civil war.

key_moments.title: Civil war victory and sweeping reforms
key_moments.text: Caesar defeated Pompey at **Pharsalus** and pursued the civil war across Egypt, North Africa, and Spain, installing **Cleopatra** and her younger brother on Egypt’s throne before crushing the last major opposition at Munda. Ruling Rome as dictator, he settled veterans in overseas colonies, enlarged the Senate with new members from Italy and the provinces, and replaced Rome’s drifting lunisolar calendar with the solar **Julian calendar**.

key_moments.title: Assassination on the Ides of March
key_moments.text: Early in the year, Caesar received the title **dictator perpetuo**—dictator in perpetuity—deepening fears among Roman aristocrats that he intended to end the Republic for good. At a Senate meeting on the **Ides of March**, conspirators including **Marcus Junius Brutus** surrounded him with drawn daggers and stabbed him twenty-three times. Suetonius notes that when Caesar’s will was unsealed, he had adopted his great-nephew **Gaius Octavius**—the future Emperor Augustus—and left money and gardens to the Roman people, helping turn public grief against the assassins.

deep_facts.text: To bring Rome’s badly drifted calendar back in line with the seasons, Caesar created the longest year in European history: **46 BC lasted 445 days**. Years of political neglect had left Roman harvest festivals falling months out of season, so Caesar—working with the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes—inserted ninety extra days into that transitional year, later dubbed **the last year of confusion**. When the new solar Julian calendar took effect on January 1, 45 BC, Cicero joked that Caesar now expected even the stars to rise by edict.

As a young man crossing the Aegean, Caesar was captured by **pirates** near the island of Pharmacusa and held for nearly forty days. Plutarch relates that when they asked for twenty talents of ransom, Caesar laughed at their ignorance of who they had caught and insisted on **fifty talents**, spending his captivity reciting poems to his captors and joking that he would return to hang them. Both Plutarch and Suetonius write that once freed he raised ships, tracked the pirates down, and crucified them—though modern historians caution that the famous story and its fifty-talent figure were likely embellished in retelling.

Caesar’s most famous dying line—**“Et tu, Brute?”**—comes from Elizabethan theater rather than Roman witnesses. **William Shakespeare** popularized the Latin phrase in his 1599 play Julius Caesar, following earlier English stage usage. Ancient accounts give a starkly different picture: Suetonius reports that Caesar pulled his robe over his head and died without speaking a word after a first groan, recording only as an unconfirmed report by others that he asked Marcus Brutus in Greek, “You too, my child?”

connections.name: Pompey
connections.connection: Caesar’s ally in the First Triumvirate became his chief rival in the civil war and was defeated at Pharsalus in 48 BC.

connections.name: Augustus
connections.connection: Caesar adopted his great-nephew Gaius Octavius in his will, launching the political rise that established the Roman Empire.

connections.name: Marcus Junius Brutus
connections.connection: Caesar’s friend and protégé joined the senatorial conspiracy that assassinated him on the Ides of March.

connections.name: Cleopatra
connections.connection: After his victory in Alexandria, Caesar placed Egypt under the rule of Cleopatra and her younger brother.

connections.name: Gallic War
connections.connection: Caesar’s prolonged military campaign in Gaul expanded Roman territory and gave him the wealth and veteran army that propelled his rise.

connections.name: Roman Republic
connections.connection: Caesar’s civil war victory and permanent dictatorship helped create the political conditions that ended the Roman Republic.

connections.name: Marcus Licinius Crassus
connections.connection: Crassus joined Caesar and Pompey in the First Triumvirate of 60 BC.

connections.name: Mark Antony
connections.connection: As consul at the time of Caesar’s murder, Antony deterred the conspirators from dragging Caesar’s body to the Tiber or revoking his decrees.

connections.name: Cicero
connections.connection: The Roman orator privately backed Senate opposition to the First Triumvirate and later joked about Caesar’s calendar reform.

connections.name: William Shakespeare
connections.connection: Shakespeare’s 1599 tragedy Julius Caesar immortalized the assassination and popularized the line “Et tu, Brute?”

findings.claim: Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman, and author who conquered Gaul and defeated Pompey in a civil war to become dictator of the Roman Republic.
findings.explanation: Wikipedia identifies Caesar as a Roman general, statesman, author, conqueror in the Gallic Wars, victor over Pompey in the civil war, and dictator of the Roman Republic.

evidence.quote: Gaius Julius Caesar[a] (12 or 13 July 100 BC – 15 March 44 BC) was a Roman general, statesman, and author who was the dictator of the Roman Republic almost continuously from 49 BC until his assassination in 44 BC. A member of the First Triumvirate, he led the Roman armies through the Gallic Wars and defeated his political rival Pompey in Caesar's civil war.
evidence.origin: English Wikipedia, Julius Caesar

findings.claim: After receiving the title dictator perpetuo, Caesar was assassinated by senators claiming to defend the Republic, which instead led to further civil wars and the rise of Augustus and the Roman Empire.
findings.explanation: Both Wikipedia and SPQR Ancient Rome document Caesar's title dictator perpetuo, his assassination by senators, and its aftermath in further civil wars and the rise of Augustus and the Roman Empire.

evidence.quote: He consolidated power and was titled as dictator perpetuo in 44 BC, helping create the political conditions that led to the collapse of the Roman Republic and the emergence of the Roman Empire.
evidence.origin: English Wikipedia, Julius Caesar

evidence.quote: A group of senators attacked him during a meeting and stabbed him repeatedly. The conspirators claimed that they were defending the Roman Republic from tyranny, but the killing failed to restore Republican government. Instead, it produced further civil wars and helped bring about the rise of Augustus and the Roman Empire.
evidence.origin: SPQR Ancient Rome, Assassination of Caesar

evidence.quote: At the end of the will, too, he adopted Gaius Octavius into his family and gave him his name.
